analysis.one_liner: Bars courts from making foreclosed homeowners repay the mortgage balance left after their home is sold.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the House in March 2014, referred to the Judiciary Committee and then a subcommittee, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a home is foreclosed and sold, the sale often does not cover the full mortgage debt. Today, in many states, the lender can go to court and get a "deficiency judgment" — a legal order making the former homeowner pay the leftover balance on a house they no longer own. This bill would have banned courts from issuing those judgments for most home loans made after the law passed, so a family that loses its home would lose the home but not also carry the remaining debt. The bill was introduced by Rep. Michelle Lujan Grisham, referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then a subcommittee, and never moved again before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners who take out a federally related mortgage after the bill takes effect and later face foreclosure. If their home sells for less than what they owe, the remaining balance would be forgiven rather than pursued in court. Families hit hardest by the housing crisis — those underwater on their mortgages — gain the most, because deficiency judgments can add tens of thousands of dollars of debt to an already devastating loss.

how_it_helps.text: After a foreclosure sale, a court could no longer order the former homeowner to pay whatever balance remained on the mortgage if the sale did not cover the full debt.

The protection covers any 'federally related mortgage loan' — the standard category that includes nearly all residential home loans — made after enactment, and it does not override state laws that are even more protective of homeowners.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and banks. They would no longer be able to collect the difference between the loan and the foreclosure sale price, which increases their losses on defaulted loans. That cost could be passed forward to future borrowers through somewhat higher rates or stricter lending standards.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies only to future loans, so no homeowner in foreclosure at the time it was proposed would have been protected; it would change behavior only for loans made after enactment.

Banning deficiency judgments means lenders bear the full loss when a foreclosed home sells for less than the debt. Lenders would likely account for that risk in pricing and underwriting, which could mean somewhat higher rates or tighter credit for future homebuyers.

The bill only prohibits the judgment itself; it does not address the foreclosure process or other costs homeowners face, and it leaves more protective state laws in place rather than setting a uniform national standard.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: families who lose a home in foreclosure would no longer face years of court-ordered payments on debt tied to a house they no longer own. The main drawback is that lenders would price in that risk, so the change would likely mean somewhat higher costs or tighter lending for future borrowers, and because it applies only to loans made after enactment, it helps no one in foreclosure today. A modest, genuinely protective rule — but one that never got any committee consideration, let alone a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, which took no action, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 27, 2014 and referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
On April 16, 2014 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law, where no further action was taken.
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders kept their power to pursue foreclosed families for the remaining loan balance, which is exactly what the bill would have taken away.

for.name: Rep. Michelle Lujan Grisham
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Foreclosure Fairness Act of 2014 on March 27, 2014.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Bob Goodlatte, R-VA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action; it was never scheduled for a markup or a vote.

against.name: Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 16, 2014 and never acted on it; no hearing or vote is recorded before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only two Democratic supporters and no Republican cosponsors, and it died without a vote in a Republican-controlled committee, so the record shows party lines but not how members would actually have voted.

industries.note: Lenders would lose the right to sue former homeowners for the unpaid balance after a foreclosure sale, so a shortfall becomes the lender's loss instead of the family's debt. That weakens their strongest collection tool on loans that go underwater.
Families who lose a home would walk away without a lingering court-ordered debt for the difference between the loan and the sale price, instead of carrying that debt for years.
